citations.quote: **Cycle notation for a finite list of distinct points.** For distinct elements $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of $X$ with $k \ge 2$, the symbol $(x_0\,x_1\,\cdots\,x_{k-1})$ denotes the permutation sending $x_i$ to $x_{i+1}$ for $i < k-1$, sending $x_{k-1}$ to $x_0$, and fixing every element of $X$ outside $\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}$.

The **symmetric group on $n$ letters** is $$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(n)=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}),$$ the group of all bijections of $n$ under composition ([[def-symmetric-group]]), with the composition convention $$(\sigma\tau)(i):=(\sigma\circ\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))\qquad(i\in n),$$ so that in a product the right-hand factor acts first.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation $$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$ where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition $(i\ i+1)$.

A ring $R$ ([[def-ring]]) is **commutative** when its multiplication is commutative ([[def-binary-operation]]): $$xy \;=\; yx \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in R .$$ Addition is commutative in every ring, by axiom (R1), so the word refers to multiplication alone.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.
Its localisation $$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$ is the **field of fractions** of $D$.
For every integral domain $D$, the localisation $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field.

A **two-sided ideal**, written $I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.
For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $R$ containing $S$.
A ring homomorphism whose kernel contains a two-sided ideal factors uniquely through the quotient ring.
For a two-sided ideal $I$, the additive cosets form a ring $R/I$ with identity $1+I$.

An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism $$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$ ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$.

citations.quote: Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $G$
be a connected smooth algebraic group scheme of finite type over $k$ (such a
$G$ is separated by Milne 1.22 and geometrically reduced, hence a classical
variety of finite type over $k$) acting on a classical variety $X$ over $k$
([[def-dimension-classical-variety]],
[[cor-smooth-variety-classical-scheme-conventions-agree]]), and let
$x\in X(k)$ be a closed point. Then: (a) every fibre over a closed $k$-point of
the orbit map $\varrho_x:G\to O_x$ is a left translate of the stabilizer $G_x$
([[lem-action-map-fibres-and-stabilizer-subscheme]]), hence has underlying
topological dimension $\dim G_x$, equivalently the dimension of its reduction;
$G_x$ may be nonreduced ([[def-dimension-noetherian-topological-space]]);
(b) $\dim G=\dim G_x+\dim O_x$; (c) the orbit closure $\overline{O_x}$ is the
union of $O_x$ and of orbits of strictly smaller dimension; consequently every
orbit of minimal dimension in $X$ is closed, and $\overline{O_x}$ contains a
closed orbit. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the generic-fibre and
constructibility inputs.

derivations.claim: **Empty chains.** If $V=0$, take $t=0$; if $e=0$ on a nonzero space, its Jordan diagram has a single column and $t=1$. In either case there are no chain variables or equations, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ is trivial and $\theta=0$. Its image is the point orbit closure, its coordinate ring is a normal domain, and the empty equation sequence is regular. The boundary is empty and has codimension $+\infty$. All conclusions follow in these cases. Henceforth $t\ge2$.

**The open chain locus.** Put $c=\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$ and $D=2\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-c$. The differential of the chain equations is $Y_iA_i+B_iX_i-X_{i-1}B_{i-1}-A_{i-1}Y_{i-1}$, with the index-zero terms zero. If each $A_i$ is injective or $B_i$ is surjective, these equations can be solved successively for any prescribed right-hand sides: use a left inverse of $A_i$ to choose $Y_i$, or a right inverse of $B_i$ to choose $X_i$, after the preceding pair is fixed. Thus the open locus $Z^\circ$ with this condition is smooth of dimension $D$ by [F4]. It is nonempty: use $U_i=\operatorname{im}e^{t-i}$, inclusions $A_i$, and restrictions $B_i=e|_{U_{i+1}}$, transported to the fixed spaces. These maps satisfy the equations and have end map $e$.

**Alternating strings and their stabilizers.** For a nilpotent pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, the odd operator $T$ on $U\oplus W$ with these components has a homogeneous Jordan-string decomposition: kernels and images of its powers are graded, so the complements in the Jordan construction may be chosen homogeneous. Every string alternates letters $a$ from $U$ and $b$ from $W$. Removing all $b$ letters gives the Jordan rows of $BA$, and removing all $a$ letters gives those of $AB$. The ranks of alternating composites recover the numbers of strings of each length and starting letter, so a diagram determines one pair orbit and there are finitely many diagrams in fixed dimensions. The pair stabilizer is the unit group of its even endomorphism algebra, an open subset of a vector space and hence smooth and irreducible. On a string $A$ kills exactly a terminal $a$ and $B$ misses exactly an initial $a$; consequently $A$ is injective iff every string ends in $b$, and $B$ is surjective iff every string begins in $b$.

**Even orbit drops.** Distinct dominated types have strictly smaller orbit dimension. One can move from a dominating partition to a dominated one by repeatedly moving a box from an earlier row to a later allowable row: choose an excess row and a subsequent deficit row, taking the last row of the source plateau and the first allowed destination to preserve the partition inequalities, and repeat until the target is reached. A move from row $i$ to row $j>i$ increases $\sum_r(2r-1)\mu_r$ by $2(j-i)$ and therefore decreases the orbit dimension by that positive even number. Each allowable unit move from row lengths $a,b$ with $a\ge b+2$ is realized by a one-parameter degeneration. On chains $u_1,\ldots,u_{a-1}$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_{b+1}$ of the destination type, keep the usual lowering maps except send $v_{b+1}$ to $v_b+z u_{a-1}$, with $v_0=0$. At $z=0$ the type is $(a-1,b+1)$; for $z\ne0$ the ranks of powers are those of $(a,b)$ (the chain generated by $v_{b+1}$ has length $a$, and the remaining chain has length $b$). Keeping other strings fixed proves that dominated types belong to the top orbit closure. Hence a drop of exactly two consists of one box moved to the next row; any other drop is at least four. Equivalently, parity also follows from $\sum_j(\mu'_j)^2\equiv\sum_j\mu'_j=N\pmod2$ for the total sum; individual summands in a difference of square sums need not be even.

**The pair-orbit dimension.** Write $m=\dim U$, $n=\dim W$, and let $E,O$ be the dimensions of the even and odd centralizers of $T$. A homomorphism between Jordan strings of lengths $L,L'$ has $\min(L,L')$ possible shifts. Counting the parity of those shifts, odd strings of the same endpoint type contribute $+1$ to the even-minus-odd count, and odd strings of opposite type contribute $-1$; the two opposite Hom directions for an odd/even pair cancel, and even/even pairs contribute zero. Summing gives $E-O=(m-n)^2$, because the difference between the numbers of odd $a$-type and odd $b$-type strings is $m-n$. The pair orbit therefore has dimension $m^2+n^2-E=\tfrac12((m+n)^2-E-O)$, half the dimension of the ordinary orbit of $T$. If a string has $r_j$ letters $a$ and $s_j$ letters $b$, then $\min(r_j+s_j,r_k+s_k)=\min(r_j,r_k)+\min(s_j,s_k)$ except for equal odd lengths with opposite endpoint types, where the left side is larger by one. Let $a_l,b_l$ count the odd strings of length $l$ beginning with the two respective letters, and put $\Delta=\sum_{l\text{ odd}}a_lb_l$. The ordinary Jordan centralizer counts now give $\dim O_{(A,B)}=mn+\tfrac12(\dim C_{BA}+\dim C_{AB})-\Delta$. This is a dimension identity for the orbit, not for the full matrix space minus the pair orbit.

**Chain strata.** Stratify $Z$ by its compatible alternating-string diagrams at every link. Compatibility means that the $b$-diagram of one link equals the $a$-diagram of the next. These are finitely many locally closed strata. Pair-orbit projections to either ordinary Jordan orbit are smooth homogeneous fibrations: their fibers are quotients of the ordinary centralizer unit group by the pair stabilizer. Both groups are smooth connected open subsets of finite-dimensional endomorphism spaces, so these fibers are irreducible. Iterating these fibrations proves each nonempty chain stratum $Z_\delta$ smooth and irreducible. The dimension at each fiber-product step is the preceding dimension plus the pair-orbit dimension minus the shared Jordan-orbit dimension. The intermediate orbit dimensions cancel in the formula of step 2.1, giving $\dim Z_\delta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12\dim C_\sigma-\sum_{i<t}\Delta_i$, where $\sigma$ is the type of its final end map.

**Dominance and the top stratum.** The chain equations make $\theta^k$ factor through $U_{t-k}$, so $\operatorname{rank}\theta^k\le n_{t-k}$ and $\theta^t=0$. Thus its type $\sigma$ is dominated by $\eta$ by [F3]. For a $b$-diagram $\sigma$, every row must first be filled internally by alternating $a$ letters; this requires exactly $|\sigma|-\ell(\sigma)$ letters, the size of the diagram obtained by deleting its first column. Over the top diagram $\eta$, this equals $n_{t-1}$, leaving no extra letters: every string starts and ends in $b$ and the lower diagram is exactly the first-column deletion of $\eta$. Repeat down the chain. There is exactly one top stratum; it has both maximal-rank maps at every link, lies in $Z^\circ$, and has every $\Delta_i=0$. Finally, expanding $q_j=n_{t-j+1}-n_{t-j}$ gives $\tfrac12\dim C_\eta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$, so its dimension is $D$.

**Drops of at least four.** By the stratum formula and the nonnegativity of all $\Delta_i$, a final orbit drop of at least four gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-4)=D-2$. Every non-top stratum has dimension at most $D-1$. This latter estimate establishes uniqueness of the dense top stratum but does not assert that every non-top stratum has codimension two: some are smooth divisors inside $Z^\circ$.

**Drops of two and the nonsmooth-locus bound.** Suppose $\sigma$ is obtained from $\eta$ by moving a box to the next row. Let $\eta'$ and $\sigma'$ denote first-column deletions and let $m=|\eta'|$, $m'=|\sigma'|$. At the last link the available number of $a$ letters is $m$ and its $a$-diagram must be dominated by $\eta'$, since its powers factor through the shorter chain. If the receiving row was nonempty, $m=m'$: internal filling consumes every $a$, all strings begin and end in $b$, and the same next-row degeneration passes to the shorter chain. If a new singleton row is created, $m=m'+1$. After internal filling there is one extra $a$. It can be attached at either end of the shortened last row, at either end of the new singleton $b$ row, or placed in a new singleton $a$ row. No earlier row can receive it: its $a$-diagram would gain a box earlier than the removed last-row box and violate dominance by $\eta'$. In the first four placements one map is maximal rank; the lower diagram is either $\eta'$ or its next-row degeneration. In the fifth placement both maps fail maximal rank, and singleton strings of both types occur, giving $\Delta_i\ge1$. This remains valid when the shortened row is itself a singleton, when there can be more than one singleton $b$. Inducting through the shorter chain shows that either every link has a maximal-rank map and $Z_\delta\subseteq Z^\circ$, or some $\Delta_i\ge1$. In the latter case the dimension formula gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-2)-1=D-2$. Together with step 5.1, this proves $\dim(Z\setminus Z^\circ)\le D-2$.

**Complete intersection and reducedness.** Every irreducible component of the scheme cut out by its $c$ equations has dimension at least $\dim M-c=D$ by [F4]. The top stratum has dimension $D$ and all other strata have smaller dimension by step 5.1, so every component has dimension $D$. Thus the equation ideal has height $c$. Its homogeneous generators form a regular sequence in the polynomial ring: at the homogeneous maximal ideal, every prefix of length $k$ has height at least $k$, since adjoining the remaining $c-k$ equations raises height by at most $c-k$; the opposite inequality is Krull's bound. Complete the generators to a system of parameters and apply the Cohen-Macaulay parameter theorem in [F4]. Homogeneous localization detects a kernel in a multiplication map, so regularity is global. The quotient is Cohen-Macaulay, hence satisfies $S_1$ and $S_2$. Every component meets the smooth open $Z^\circ$ by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_0$; [F5] implies reducedness.

**Irreducibility and normality of the chain.** The unique top stratum is irreducible. Its closure contains every component: otherwise a component of dimension $D$ would have a nonempty open subset outside that closure, contained in a finite union of strata of dimensions at most $D-1$, which is impossible. Thus the reduced chain ring is a domain. Its singular locus is contained in $Z\setminus Z^\circ$, of codimension at least two by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_1$; it satisfies $S_2$ by step 7.1. Serre's criterion [F5] gives normality.

**The invariant quotient.** For one pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, invariants under $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ are generated by entries of $AB$: the scalar matrices force equal polynomial degrees in $A,B$, polarization turns a bihomogeneous invariant into a mixed tensor invariant, and [F6] expresses it as permutation contractions. Each contraction is a product of entries of $AB$, with possible cyclic traces also polynomials in those entries. For rational finite-dimensional $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ modules, the central scalar torus splits the space into integer weight spaces. On each weight space apply the semisimple Lie algebra complete-reducibility theorem [F6] to $\mathfrak{sl}(U)$; an invariant complement then respects the center as well. It respects the group because elementary unipotents and diagonal matrices generate $\mathrm{GL}(U)$. Thus rational quotient invariants lift by complete reducibility in bounded polynomial degree, so the same description applies to a stable closed subscheme with its induced relations. Eliminate vertices in order. At the first vertex the invariant generators are $A_1B_1$ and the remaining variables; the chain equation replaces $A_1B_1$ by $B_2A_2$. The quotient is consequently the graph over the remaining variables with the induced rank and nilpotency relations, and eliminating the next vertex applies the same one-pair calculation. Repeating leaves precisely the entries of $\theta$. Thus $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is generated by those entries, and is the coordinate ring of the closure of $\theta(Z)$. The rank bounds of step 4.1 put the image in the orbit closure of $e$, while the inclusion/restriction construction of step 1.2, applied to every conjugate of $e$, puts its full orbit in the image. Hence that closure is $X$ and $\mathbb C[Z]^H\cong\mathbb C[X]$.

**Normality and boundary of the orbit closure.** An element of $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[Z]^H)$ integral over $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is also integral over the normal domain $\mathbb C[Z]$, hence belongs to it. Being a fraction of invariant elements it is fixed by $H$, so it belongs to $\mathbb C[Z]^H$; no equality between the full invariant fraction field and the fraction field of the invariant ring is needed. Therefore $\mathbb C[X]$ is a normal domain, reduced and irreducible. The finitely many boundary nilpotent orbits have positive even dimension drops by step 1.4, so their union has codimension at least two. The point cases and their empty boundary were proved in step 1.1. This proves all chain and orbit conclusions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ ([[def-nilpotent-endomorphism]]),
let $X=\overline{\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e}$ be the closure in
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ of its conjugacy orbit
([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), and let
$\partial X=X\setminus\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e$. Then $\mathbb C[X]$ is a reduced
irreducible normal domain and $\operatorname{codim}_X\partial X\ge2$. This
holds for every Jordan type, not only the regular nilpotent cone.

The proof uses the *chain schemes*: if the Jordan partition of $e$ has column
lengths $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, put $n_i=q_t+\cdots+q_{t-i+1}$ and
$U_i=\mathbb C^{n_i}$ for $0\le i\le t$. Let $M=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(U_i,U_{i+1})\times\operatorname{Hom}(U_{i+1},U_i)\bigr)$
with coordinates $(A_i,B_i)$ and let $Z\subseteq M$ be the closed subscheme
$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$ when $t\ge2$. For the empty Jordan diagram ($V=0$,
$t=0$) and the single-column diagram ($e=0$, $t=1$), the chain has no
variables or equations: take $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ trivial
and $\theta=0$; the equation list above is imposed only on existing links.
In these cases $X$ is a point, its boundary is empty, and its boundary
codimension is $+\infty$.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every commutative Noetherian integrally closed domain satisfies $(S_2)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring and let $M\ne0$ be a finite
$R$-module. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}(M)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}_R(M).$$

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $M$ be a finitely generated left
$R$-module, and let $S \subseteq R$ be multiplicative. Then
$$ \operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}M)=\{S^{-1}\mathfrak p : \mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M),\ \mathfrak p \cap S=\varnothing\}. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be Noetherian, let $M$ be finite, let $I$ lie in the Jacobson radical,
and let $x\in I$ be $M$-regular. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}_I(M/xM)=\operatorname{depth}_I(M)-1,$$
with $\infty-1=\infty$.

Assume Dependent Choice. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Then
the set of zero divisors on $M$ is
$$ \bigcup_{\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M)}\mathfrak p. $$
If the Axiom of Choice also holds and $M$ is finitely generated, this is a finite union.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ be an ideal, and let
$\mathfrak p_1,\dots,\mathfrak p_n$ be prime ideals with $n \ge 1$. If
$$ I\subseteq \mathfrak p_1\cup\cdots\cup \mathfrak p_n, $$
then $I\subseteq \mathfrak p_i$ for some $i$.

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, let $n\ge0$, and let
$E:=V^{\otimes n}$ carry the left place action of $S_n$
([[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]). Let $A$ be
the image of the algebra homomorphism $\mathbb C[S_n]\to\operatorname{End}(E)$
extending the place action, and let
$B:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$
be the linear span of the diagonal operators
$g^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n$.
Then:

1. **(Mutual centralizers.)** $B=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F a=aF\text{ for
   all }a\in A\}$ and $A=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F b=bF\text{ for all
   }b\in B\}$.
2. **(Uniqueness of the identification.)** $B$ is a unital
   $\mathbb C$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$ and equals the image of
   the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
   $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$, that is the unital subalgebra generated by the
   operators $\Delta(T)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes
   \mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}$, $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$
   ([[lem-tensor-place-operators-span-the-symmetric-centralizer]]).

All statements include $n=0$, where $E=\mathbb C$.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

derivations.claim: **The zero-dimensional case.** If $V=0$, its orbit closure is a point and its boundary is empty by [F1]. For $d=0$, $V^{\otimes d}=\mathbb C$ and every fixed operator is a scalar, extended by the constant polynomial map; the empty permutation and empty tensor product give the asserted normal form. For $d>0$, $V^{\otimes d}=0$ and its endomorphism space has only the zero operator, extended by the zero map; the normal form is the empty sum. Thus both assertions hold without a largest Jordan block. Henceforth $V\ne0$, so its largest block length $l$ exists.

Hartogs lifting. Let $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $f\in\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ be regular on $O$, hence regular off a closed subset of $X\setminus O$; since $\partial X$ has codimension $\ge2$ in $X$ by the normality lemma [F1], $f$ is regular in codimension $1$ and therefore extends to $A$ by [F2]. Applying this coordinatewise to maps into a finite-dimensional vector space shows that every regular map $O\to W$ into a finite-dimensional vector space extends uniquely to a regular map $X\to W$.

The equivariant map on $O$. Fix $B\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})^{G_e}$ and define, for $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $F(g\,e\,g^{-1}):=(g^{\otimes d})\,B\,(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. This is well defined: if $g_1e g_1^{-1}=g_2eg_2^{-1}$, then $g_2^{-1}g_1\in G_e$, so $(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{\otimes d}B(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{-\otimes d}=B$ by $G_e$-invariance, which rearranges to $(g_1^{\otimes d})B(g_1^{-1})^{\otimes d}=(g_2^{\otimes d})B(g_2^{-1})^{\otimes d}$. The map $F$ is $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant by construction: $F(hXh^{-1})=(h^{\otimes d})F(X)(h^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ for $X\in O$.

Regularity of $F$ on $O$. The ranks of $X^0,X^1,\dots,X^{l-1}$ are constant on $O$. Cover $O$ by open charts where fixed minors used to select bases of the kernels and images, their quotient complements and Jordan top vectors are nonzero. Gaussian elimination on such a chart gives a Jordan basis for $X$ with entries regular in $X$. Let $g(X)$ carry a fixed Jordan basis for $e$ to this chosen Jordan basis for $X$, with the same ordered string lengths. Then $g(X)e g(X)^{-1}=X$. Restricting to the open chart where the Jordan-basis determinant is nonzero makes both $g(X)$ and $g(X)^{-1}$ regular, since their entries have only the fixed nonvanishing minors and determinant as denominators. Thus $X\mapsto(g(X)^{\otimes d})B(g(X)^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ is the map of step 1.3 and is regular on each chart. These charts cover $O$; on overlaps $g_2(X)^{-1}g_1(X)\in G_e$, so the expressions agree by $G_e$-invariance of $B$. Hence $F$ is regular on $O$.

Extension to $X$. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the map $F\colon O\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ is a regular equivariant map on the dense orbit; by step 1.2 it extends uniquely to a regular map $F\colon X\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. Since $\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[\operatorname{End}(V)]/I(X)$ and $X$ is an affine closed subset of the affine space $\operatorname{End}(V)$, the coordinate functions of $F$ are restrictions of polynomial functions on $\operatorname{End}(V)$; fixing representatives gives a polynomial map $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ extending $F$.

Equivariance of $\Phi$. For fixed $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, both sides of $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ are polynomial maps in $X$; they agree on the dense orbit $O$ by step 1.3 and hence on all of $X$. Consequently the class of $\Phi$ in the finite-dimensional space of polynomial maps $\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ of degree at most $K$ (for $K$ at least the degree of $\Phi$), modulo the $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-stable subspace of maps vanishing on $X$, is invariant for the conjugation action. By the invariant-lifting property of complete reducibility [F3], this class has an invariant representative $\Phi'$ of degree at most $K$; then $\Phi'$ is a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map on $\operatorname{End}(V)$ agreeing with $F$ on $X$, and $\Phi'(e)=F(e)=B$ since $e\in O$, which is assertion (1).

Polarization. Write $\Phi=\sum_k\Phi_k$ for its homogeneous components of degree $k$; each $\Phi_k$ is equivariant. Fix $k$ and assume for the structure argument that $\Phi$ is homogeneous of degree $k$. Polarize the $k$ matrix variables $X_1,\dots,X_k$ of $\Phi$ and pair the output in $\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ with $d$ independent matrices $Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ using the nondegenerate trace pairing on each tensor factor; this produces a multilinear $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-invariant $P(X_1,\dots,X_k;Y_1,\dots,Y_d)\in\mathbb C$ in $(k+d)$ matrix arguments.

Tensor invariants are permutation contractions. By the Schur-Weyl description [F3], every multilinear invariant of the matrix arguments is a linear combination of contractions: each argument contributes one upper and one lower index, an invariant pairs each upper index with a lower index of another argument, and the invariant is a product over the cycles of the resulting permutation of traces of the corresponding cyclically ordered product of matrices.

Covariant normal form. Depolarize in the $k$ identical variables $X_i=X$ and read each contraction cycle. A cycle that uses only $X$-arguments contributes a scalar invariant polynomial in $X$; a cycle that uses some $Y$-arguments alternates blocks of $X$'s and single $Y$'s, so its trace is precisely the trace pairing of $Y_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Y_d$ with a place permutation of $X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d}$. By nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, the operator identity $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ follows, with $h_i\ge0$, $\sigma_h$ a place permutation and $c_h$ a scalar invariant polynomial (a polynomial in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^m)$); summing over the homogeneous components gives assertion (2).

Evaluation at $e$. Since $e^l=0$ for the largest Jordan block length $l$ of $e$, evaluating the normal form at $X=e$ kills every term with some $h_i\ge l$; the surviving terms are place permutations applied to a tensor product of nonnegative powers $e^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{h_d}$ multiplied by the scalar invariants $c_h(e)$, which are ordinary numbers depending only on the Jordan type of $e$ (that is, on the list of eigenvalues $\operatorname{tr}(e^m)$, all zero for nilpotent $e$, so $c_h(e)=c_h(0)$). This gives the concrete description of the $G_e$-fixed endomorphisms used by the double centralizer theorem.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

For every finite-dimensional representation $\rho:\mathfrak g\to
\mathfrak{gl}(V)$, the trace form is bilinear and symmetric, and it is
invariant in the sense that

$$B_\rho([z,x],y)+B_\rho(x,[z,y])=0.$$

Consequently the Killing form has all three properties.

$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a Lie algebra over $k$. In $T(\mathfrak g)$, regard
$[x,y]\in\mathfrak g$ as an element of tensor degree one, and let $I$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by

$$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\qquad(x,y\in\mathfrak g).$$

The **universal enveloping algebra** is

$$U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$

Write

$$\iota_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow U(\mathfrak g)$$

for the composite of the degree-one inclusion with the quotient map. This
definition makes $U(\mathfrak g)$ a unital associative algebra and $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ a
linear map. It does not assert that $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ is injective; that conclusion will
come from PBW.

For a vector space $V$ over $k$, write

$$\mathfrak{gl}(V)=\operatorname{End}_k(V)$$

with commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Expansion of triple composites shows
that this is a Lie algebra in every characteristic.

A **representation** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ on $V$ is a Lie-algebra
homomorphism

$$\rho:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak{gl}(V).$$

Writing $xv$ for $\rho(x)(v)$, this is equivalently a $k$-bilinear action
$\mathfrak g\times V\to V$ satisfying

$$[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$$

for all $x,y\in\mathfrak g$ and $v\in V$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis is
imposed on either $\mathfrak g$ or $V$. The zero vector space and the zero
action are allowed.

derivations.claim: The endomorphism $e$ acts on the box basis by $ev_i=v_{L(i)}$ and $ev_i=0$ for boxes with $L(i)=\emptyset$; hence the $v_i$ in one row form a Jordan string of length $p_i$, because left shifts run from the rightmost box of the row to the first. Consequently $e$ is nilpotent of Jordan type $\lambda=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$, $e\in\mathfrak g_1$, and the number of columns is $l=p_n$ when the row list is nonempty, with $l=0$ for the empty row list. Zero-length rows contribute no Jordan strings; for $N=0$ all box-indexed sums and vector spaces are empty or zero.

Parabolic structure. The degree defines a $\mathbb Z$-grading of the associative algebra: $\deg(e_{h,k}e_{k',l})=\deg e_{h,k}+\deg e_{k',l}$ when $k=k'$ by [F1], and $[\mathfrak g_r,\mathfrak g_s]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{r+s}$. Hence $\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r$ is a subalgebra, its degree-zero part $\mathfrak h$ consists of the matrices $e_{h,k}$ with $\mathrm{col}(h)=\mathrm{col}(k)$, which is exactly the block-diagonal subalgebra with blocks of sizes $q_1,\dots,q_l$, so $\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$; the strictly positive part $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$ is a nilpotent ideal and $\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r$ is the nilradical of the opposite parabolic, with $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak m\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$.

The centralizer basis. First $[e,e_{h,k}]=e_{L(h),k}-e_{h,R(k)}$ for boxes $h,k$, with a term omitted when the relevant neighbour is absent (this is $[e,e_{h,k}]=\sum_d(e_{L(d),d}e_{h,k}-e_{h,k}e_{L(d),d})$ and $e_{L(d),d}e_{h,k}=\delta_{d,h}e_{L(d),k}$, while $e_{h,k}e_{L(d),d}=\delta_{L(d),k}e_{h,d}$ and $L(d)=k$ holds exactly for $d=R(k)$ in the same row). Now write $e_{i,j;r}=\sum_ce_{h_c,k_c}$ with $h_c$ the box of row $i$ in column $c$ and $k_c$ the box of row $j$ in column $c+r$, the sum over $c$ with $1\le c\le p_i$ and $1\le c+r\le p_j$; here $r\ge s_{i,j}\ge0$ by the defining range, so this index set is exactly $c=1,\dots,\min(p_i,p_j-r)$. Then $[e,e_{i,j;r}]=\sum_c(e_{h_{c-1},k_c}-e_{h_c,k_{c+1}})$ where a term is omitted when the neighbour does not exist; shifting the second sum by $c\mapsto c+1$ and using $R(k_c)=k_{c+1}$ (which exists exactly when $c+r<p_j$) shows that the two sums run over the same index set $\{c:c\ge2,\ c\le\min(p_i,p_j-r)\}$, because for every $c$ in the defining range one has $c+r\le p_j$; hence the commutator is $0$. The $e_{i,j;r}$ are linearly independent because they are sums over pairwise disjoint matrix units, and their number is $\sum_{i,j}\#\{r:s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}=\sum_{i,j}(p_j-\max(0,p_j-p_i))=\sum_{i,j}\min(p_i,p_j)$, which equals $\dim\mathfrak g^e$ by [F2]. Hence they form a basis of $\mathfrak g^e$.

The bijection $J\to K$. For $(a,b)\in J$ put $i=\mathrm{row}(a)$, $j=\mathrm{row}(b)$ and $r=\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)$. Because $b$ is rightmost, $\mathrm{col}(b)=p_j$; hence $r=p_j-\mathrm{col}(a)\ge0$, $r<p_j$ because $\mathrm{col}(a)\ge1$, and $r\ge p_j-p_i$ because $\mathrm{col}(a)\le p_i$. Thus $s_{i,j}=\max(0,p_j-p_i)\le r<p_j$, so the map lands in $K$. The triple determines $b$ as the rightmost box of row $j$ and $a$ as the box of row $i$ in column $p_j-r$, proving injectivity. Conversely, if $(i,j,r)\in K$, then $r<p_j$ gives $1\le p_j-r$, while $r\ge\max(0,p_j-p_i)$ gives $p_j-r\le p_i$. Thus those two boxes exist, their columns satisfy $\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b)$, and they give the required preimage. If either row has length zero, the index range in $K$ is empty, consistently with the absence of such a box pair.

The character. For $x,y\in\mathfrak m$ one has $[x,y]\in[\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{\le-2}$ by step 1.2, and $e\in\mathfrak g_1$, so $[x,y]e\in\mathfrak g_{\le-1}$ and $\operatorname{tr}([x,y]e)=0$ by [F3]. Hence $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$, that is, $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character on $\mathfrak m$: for $x,y\in\mathfrak m$, $\chi([x,y])=\operatorname{tr}([x,y]e)=0$.

The good-grading conditions. By step 1.3, the centralizer $\mathfrak g^e$ has a homogeneous basis $e_{i,j;r}$ with $r\ge s_{i,j}\ge0$, so it has no negative-degree part. The kernel of $\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_r\to\mathfrak g_{r+1}$ is $\mathfrak g^e\cap\mathfrak g_r$, hence this map is injective for $r<0$. The trace pairing is nondegenerate between $\mathfrak g_r$ and $\mathfrak g_{-r}$: each matrix unit $e_{a,b}$ pairs with $e_{b,a}$, and matrix units of other total degree have zero trace. Invariance gives $\operatorname{tr}([e,x]y)=-\operatorname{tr}(x[e,y])$, so the transpose of the map on degree $r$ is, up to sign, $\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_{-r-1}\to\mathfrak g_{-r}$. For $r\ge0$ the latter is injective by the negative-degree result; finite-dimensional duality therefore makes the original map surjective. These are the good-grading conditions for degree-one $e$. They remain valid when $e=0$, because all nonzero spaces then have degree zero.

The identity $\xi_{a,b}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)}$. Left shifts of $a$ run through the boxes of row $i$ in columns $\mathrm{col}(a),\mathrm{col}(a)-1,\dots,1$, and the corresponding left shifts of $b$ run through the boxes of row $j$ in columns $\mathrm{col}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-1,\dots,\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)+1$; all these exist because $\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)+1\ge1$ and the shifts stop while the row $i$ box exists. The pairs $(\mathrm{row}(h),\mathrm{row}(k))$ obtained are exactly the pairs $(i,j)$ with column difference $\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)$ and $\mathrm{col}(h)$ ranging over $1,\dots,\mathrm{col}(a)$; by step 2.1 these are exactly the pairs indexing $e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)}$. Hence the two finite sums coincide, and the two displayed families are the same basis of $\mathfrak g^e$.

Dynkin normalization and the zero boundary. If $e\ne0$, step 1.1 puts this nonzero element in pyramid degree $1$, whereas the standard Dynkin grading defined by an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple has $[h,e]=2e$ and puts it in degree $2$; these two gradings therefore differ. There is no assertion that every Dynkin matrix degree is even: on Jordan strings of lengths one and two the standard $h$-weights are $0$ and $1,-1$, so matrix units between these strings have odd weights. If $e=0$, no row has length greater than one, since a row of length at least two contributes a distinct nonzero left-shift matrix unit. Hence all boxes lie in the first column or there are none, every matrix unit has pyramid degree zero, and the zero triple gives the trivial Dynkin grading as well. If $N=0$, there are no matrix units or centralizer indices; the parabolic, Levi, opposite nilradical and trace character are zero. Thus the conventions and good-grading conditions cover repeated row lengths, zero-length rows and the empty pyramid without an exclusion.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the Casimir element of
[[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
and its operator on every $\mathfrak g$-module is the image under the
representation, commuting with the $\mathfrak g$-action
([[lem-the-casimir-operator-is-basis-independent-and-intertwining]],
[[lem-the-casimir-element-is-independent-of-dual-bases]]).

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $0\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$ (so $z_M$ acts as the representation of the
central element $z$ of $\mathfrak g$).

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

Let $M$ be a right $R$-module, let ${}_RN_S$ be an $(R,S)$-bimodule, and let $P$ be a left $S$-module. There is a canonical group isomorphism

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}:(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\longrightarrow M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$$

determined by

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}((m\otimes n)\otimes p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$

It respects any compatible outer module actions and is natural in $M,N,P$.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Work over the field $\mathbb C$ and fix an integer $d\ge 0$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-commutative-ring]]). Let
$\mathcal F_d$ be the free associative unital $\mathbb C$-algebra on the
$d+(d-1)$ symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ (for $d=0$ there is only
the unit; for $d=1$ only $x_1$), with its word basis and universal property
([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]), and let
$I_d\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}\mathcal F_d$ be the two-sided ideal
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]])
generated by the following elements:

- $x_ix_j-x_jx_i$ for all $1\le i,j\le d$;
- $s_i^2-1$, $s_is_{i+1}s_i-s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$, and $s_is_j-s_js_i$ for
  $|i-j|>1$, for $1\le i,j\le d-1$;
- $s_ix_j-x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i-1$, and
  $x_{i+1}s_i-s_ix_i-1$, for $1\le i\le d-1$ and $1\le j\le d$.

The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** is the quotient $\mathbb C$-algebra
$$H_d:=\mathcal F_d/I_d$$
with unit element written $1$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]). We keep the symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ for their images, and for $w\in S_d$ we write
$w$ for the image in $H_d$ of any word in the $s_i$ representing $w$; this is
independent of the chosen word once the basis theorem below is proved. For
$a\in\mathbb C$, the notation $H_d/(x_1-a)$ means the quotient by the two-sided
ideal generated by $x_1-a$.

The verification below establishes exactly the structure of $H_d$ used
throughout this page: the ordered monomials
$$x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w,\qquad r_1,\dots,r_d\ge0,\ w\in S_d,$$
form a $\mathbb C$-basis, so that
$H_d\cong\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]$ as a vector
space with polynomial and group-algebra subalgebras
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-group-ring]]);
$H_0=\mathbb C$ and $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$; for every $a$ there is a unique
algebra isomorphism
$$H_d/(x_1-a)\cong\mathbb C[S_d],\qquad x_j\longmapsto a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j);$$
and total polynomial degree is an algebra filtration whose associated graded is
the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which
$s_i$ acts by swapping $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. For $d\ge2$, the cross relation is
inhomogeneous, so it does not turn $H_d$ into a graded algebra with
$\deg x_i=1$ and $\deg s_i=0$. For $d=0$ the algebra $\mathbb C$ has its
degree-zero grading, and for $d=1$ the algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ has its
natural polynomial grading.

The Casimir element $\Omega_B$ is independent of the chosen dual bases and
belongs to the center of $U(\mathfrak g)$. Consequently its action on every
$\mathfrak g$-module is a $\mathfrak g$-intertwiner.

For a vector space $V$ over $k$, write

$$\mathfrak{gl}(V)=\operatorname{End}_k(V)$$

with commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Expansion of triple composites shows
that this is a Lie algebra in every characteristic.

A **representation** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ on $V$ is a Lie-algebra
homomorphism

$$\rho:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak{gl}(V).$$

Writing $xv$ for $\rho(x)(v)$, this is equivalently a $k$-bilinear action
$\mathfrak g\times V\to V$ satisfying

$$[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$$

for all $x,y\in\mathfrak g$ and $v\in V$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis is
imposed on either $\mathfrak g$ or $V$. The zero vector space and the zero
action are allowed.

derivations.claim: The infinitesimal braid identities. For distinct labels $a,b,c$ one has $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}+\Omega_{bc}]=0$: expanding $\Omega=\sum E_{uv}\otimes E_{vu}$ and using [F3], the double commutator sum splits into terms $[E_{uv},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{vu}\otimes E_{yx}$ and $E_{uv}\otimes[E_{vu},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{yx}$, and the two resulting sums cancel term by term after relabelling; equivalently, this is the identity $[\Omega_{12},\Omega_{13}+\Omega_{23}]=0$ in $U(\mathfrak g)^{\otimes3}$, which is the derivative of the invariance of $\Omega$ under the diagonal adjoint action. Consequently $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}]=-[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{bc}]=[\Omega_{ac},\Omega_{bc}]$. In particular, for three natural factors this is the identity $[P_{ab},P_{ac}]+[P_{ab},P_{bc}]=0$ for the flips.

The Coxeter relations for $s_i$. $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ is an involution; $s_is_j=s_js_i$ for $|i-j|>1$ because the pairs of interchanged labels are disjoint; and $s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$ because both sides are the permutation operator inducing the same permutation of the three labelled factors.

Cross relations. Conjugation by $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ interchanges the labels $i$ and $i+1$ in any operator supported on those factors, so $s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i$ and $s_iP_{k,i+1}=P_{ki}s_i$ for $k<i$. Therefore $s_ix_{i+1}=s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}+\sum_{k<i}s_iP_{k,i+1}+s_iP_{i,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}s_i+1=x_is_i+1$, and symmetrically $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$. For $j<i$, all labels in $x_j$ are disjoint from $\{i,i+1\}$, so $s_i$ commutes with every summand. For $j>i+1$, $\Omega_{0j}$ and the terms $P_{kj}$ with $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ commute with $s_i$, while conjugation by $s_i$ interchanges $P_{ij}$ and $P_{i+1,j}$. Their sum is invariant, so again $s_ix_j=x_js_i$; the two overlapping summands need not commute individually.

Polynomial commutation. Fix $i<j$. Since $x_i=\Omega_{0i}+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}$ and $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{l<j}P_{lj}$, the commutator is $[\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{l<j}[\Omega_{0i},P_{lj}]+\sum_{k<i}[P_{ki},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{k<i}\sum_{l<j}[P_{ki},P_{lj}]$. The second sum reduces to the single term $[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}]$ (all other $P_{lj}$ are disjoint from the labels $0,i$), and the third sum vanishes (all pairs $\{k,i\}$, $\{0,j\}$ are disjoint since $k<i<j$). In the fourth sum only the terms with $k=l$ or $l=i$ can fail to vanish, so it equals $\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. Hence $[x_i,x_j]=([\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}])+\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. The first bracket vanishes by step 1.1 with $a=0$, $b=i$, $c=j$ together with $\Omega_{ij}=P_{ij}$; each summand of the second bracket vanishes by step 1.1 for the three distinct labels $k,i,j$. Therefore $[x_i,x_j]=0$.

Naturality, commutation with $\mathfrak g$, and the right action. The place permutations are natural in $M$ and commute with $\mathfrak g$; the Casimir operators are intertwiners by [F5]; hence every $x_j$ and $s_i$ is natural and $\mathfrak g$-linear. The relations established in steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the defining relations of $H_d$ [F4], so the assignment $x_j\mapsto x_j$, $s_i\mapsto s_i$ defines a left $H_d$-action. The generator-fixing anti-automorphism $\omega$ of $H_d$ (which preserves each defining relation because the reversed cross relation $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$ is also a defining relation) converts it into a right action by $e\cdot u:=\rho(\omega(u))e$; the anti-automorphism property gives $(e\cdot u)\cdot v=\rho(\omega(v))\rho(\omega(u))e=\rho(\omega(uv))e=e\cdot(uv)$. This proves both assertions.

citations.quote:
Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N\ge0$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, where $l=p_n$ for a
nonempty row list and $l=0$ for an empty row list. Zero-length rows have no
boxes. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put

citations.quote:
An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the Casimir element of
[[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
and its operator on every $\mathfrak g$-module is the image under the
representation, commuting with the $\mathfrak g$-action
([[lem-the-casimir-operator-is-basis-independent-and-intertwining]],
[[lem-the-casimir-element-is-independent-of-dual-bases]]).

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $0\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$ (so $z_M$ acts as the representation of the
central element $z$ of $\mathfrak g$).

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ ([[def-nilpotent-endomorphism]]),
let $X=\overline{\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e}$ be the closure in
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ of its conjugacy orbit
([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), and let
$\partial X=X\setminus\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e$. Then $\mathbb C[X]$ is a reduced
irreducible normal domain and $\operatorname{codim}_X\partial X\ge2$. This
holds for every Jordan type, not only the regular nilpotent cone.

The proof uses the *chain schemes*: if the Jordan partition of $e$ has column
lengths $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, put $n_i=q_t+\cdots+q_{t-i+1}$ and
$U_i=\mathbb C^{n_i}$ for $0\le i\le t$. Let $M=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(U_i,U_{i+1})\times\operatorname{Hom}(U_{i+1},U_i)\bigr)$
with coordinates $(A_i,B_i)$ and let $Z\subseteq M$ be the closed subscheme
$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$ when $t\ge2$. For the empty Jordan diagram ($V=0$,
$t=0$) and the single-column diagram ($e=0$, $t=1$), the chain has no
variables or equations: take $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ trivial
and $\theta=0$; the equation list above is imposed only on existing links.
In these cases $X$ is a point, its boundary is empty, and its boundary
codimension is $+\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, let
$G_e=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}(V):geg^{-1}=e\}$ be its centralizer, and let $d\ge0$.

1. Every $G_e$-fixed endomorphism $B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V^{\otimes d})$
   is the value at $e$ of a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map
   $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$
   (polynomial in the matrix entries of the input, with
   $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$).
2. Every such equivariant polynomial map is a finite sum
   $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ with
   $h_i\ge0$, where $\sigma_h$ is a place permutation of the $d$ tensor
   factors and $c_h$ is an invariant scalar polynomial in $X$ (a polynomial
   in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^k)$).

The extension in (1) is proved by Hartogs lifting on the normal codimension-$\ge2$
orbit closure; the structure in (2) is proved by polarization and the
Schur-Weyl description of tensor invariants, not by importing a
first-fundamental-theorem for the full matrix algebra.

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this

of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators

Let $N\ge1$, let $M$ be a $\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$-module, let
$V=\mathbb C^N$ be the natural module, and on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ use the
operators $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ of
[[def-arakawa-suzuki-casimir-operators-on-tensor-functors]]. Then:

1. The operators $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ commute with the
   $\mathfrak g$-action and are natural in $M$, and satisfy all the defining
   relations of the degenerate affine Hecke algebra
   [[def-degenerate-affine-hecke-algebra]]: the Coxeter relations for the
   $s_i$; $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ and

derivations.claim: The first centralizer. An operator $T\in\operatorname{End}(E)$ commutes with the action of $B$ if and only if it commutes with the individual $e$-operators and with the place permutations: the first condition says $T\in A^{\otimes d}$ by [F2], and then the second says $T\in(A^{\otimes d})^{S_d}$, which is spanned by the elements $a^{\otimes d}$, $a\in A$. The image of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$ under the diagonal representation is contained in $\operatorname{End}_B(E)$: the diagonal action of $A$ commutes with the individual $e$'s and with places. Conversely, for $a\in A$ the element $a^{\otimes d}$ is the value at $1$ of the diagonal action of $\sum_ka_k^{\otimes d}$; Newton's identities express the product $a_1\cdots a_d$ of the commuting operators $a_i=1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes a\otimes1^{\otimes(d-i)}$ as a polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ in the power sums $p_k=\sum_ia_i^k$, $1\le k\le d$, and each $p_k$ is the image under $\varphi$ of $a^k\in U(\mathfrak g^e)$. Hence $a^{\otimes d}\in\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))$ and $\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))=\operatorname{End}_B(E)$.

The second centralizer. An operator $T$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action if and only if it is $G_e$-fixed, because $G_e=A^\times$ generates $A$ linearly in the diagonal representation: differentiating $t\mapsto(1+ta)^{\otimes d}$ at $t=0$ recovers the diagonal action of $a$, and Newton-type generation is not needed for this direction. By [F3] every $G_e$-fixed operator is $\Phi(e)$ for an equivariant polynomial covariant $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$; evaluating at $X=e$ replaces each $X^{h_i}$ by $e^{h_i}$, which is a polynomial in the individual $e$-operators of degree less than $l$, so $\Phi(e)\in\psi(B)$ (the truncated algebra $B$ contains exactly the polynomials $e^0,\dots,e^{l-1}$ in each factor and the places). Conversely every element of $\psi(B)$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action: for $a\in A$ put $\Delta_d(a)=\sum_{k=1}^d a^{(k)}$; each individual $e^{(j)}$ satisfies $[\Delta_d(a),e^{(j)}]=[a,e]^{(j)}=0$, and each place permutation $P_\sigma$ satisfies $P_\sigma\Delta_d(a)P_\sigma^{-1}=\Delta_d(a)$. These operators generate $\psi(B)$, so their products and linear combinations also commute with every $\Delta_d(a)$. Therefore $\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g^e}(E)^{\mathrm{op}}=\psi(B)$.

Stable injectivity. Suppose $e$ has at least $d$ Jordan strings of the maximum length $l$, with top vectors $w_1,\dots,w_d$ on distinct strings. The vectors $w_1^{r_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes w_d^{r_d}$ with $0\le r_i<l$ (where $w^r=e^rw$ is the $r$-th vector of the string) are $l^d$ distinct members of the Jordan tensor basis of $E$; applying the $d!$ place permutations gives $l^d d!$ distinct basis vectors, since the string label of each tensor factor is recovered from the vector and the place permutation is recovered from the ordering of the labels. These vectors span a right $B$-submodule isomorphic to the regular module $B$ (the basis vectors $e^{r_1}w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{r_d}w_d\sigma$, $\sigma\in S_d$, multiply exactly as the standard basis of the truncated polynomial/permutation algebra), so the right action $\psi$ is injective. For $d=0$, $E=\mathbb C$, $B=\mathbb C$ and both identities and injectivity reduce to scalar identities.
